title: Hyperparameter Transfer Laws for Non-Recurrent Multi-Path Neural Networks
claim: Prior work gives depth-scaling rules only for sequential or special-case networks; ours gives one universal law across diverse architectures.
layout: 2 panels, left prior stacked vs right ours; dashed lines expand a node into three architectures
description: The figure has two panels split by a vertical line. Panel (a), 'Prior work', stacks three rows separated by dashed lines: a sequential MLP drawn as yellow nodes with unit-depth tick marks, a ResNet with 1-layer blocks and skip connections, and a Transformer that is analyzed only under width scaling (d to D). Each row ends with a formula for the optimal learning rate: L^(-3/2), L^(-1/2) and W^(-1). Panel (b), 'Our work', shows a chain of green nodes. Dashed lines from one node expand into three rounded boxes: CNN on CIFAR-100, ResNet on ImageNet and Vision Transformer on CIFAR-10. Each box has a block diagram with depth-unit counts and a log-log scatter plot with a red dashed fit line. A single L^(-3/2) formula sits below the three boxes. Yellow marks prior work and green marks ours.
caption: Overview of prior work and our results on depth-wise learning-rate scaling. 1 denotes one depth unit, d and D denote width. (a) Prior work mainly analyzes sequential networks or special cases, and Transformers are often discussed only under width scaling. (b) We treat CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers as non-recurrent multi-path networks and obtain a unified depth law for the maximal-update learning rate.
abstract: Deeper modern architectures are costly to train, making hyperparameter transfer preferable to expensive repeated tuning. Maximal Update Parametrization ($Î¼$P) helps explain why many hyperparameters transfer across width. Yet depth scaling is less understood for modern architectures, whose computation graphs contain multiple parallel paths and residual aggregation. To unify various non-recurrent multi-path neural networks such as CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers, we introduce a graph-based notion of effective depth. Under stabilizing initializations and a maximal-update criterion, we show that the optimal learning rate decays with effective depth following a universal -3/2 power law. Here, the maximal-update criterion maximizes the typical one-step representation change at initialization without causing instability, and effective depth is the minimal path length from input to output, counting layers and residual additions. Experiments across diverse architectures confirm the predicted slope and enable reliable zero-shot transfer of learning rates across depths and widths, turning depth scaling into a predictable hyperparameter-transfer problem.
